title: The Devout Tray-Maker and His Wife
summary: In a quiet alley of Damascus lived an honest artisan named Abu Ahmad who carved wooden trays and platters from walnut and olive wood. He was a master of his craft; each tray was...
keywords: the devout tray-maker and his wife
full_text:
In a quiet alley of Damascus lived an honest artisan named Abu Ahmad who carved wooden trays and platters from walnut and olive wood. He was a master of his craft; each tray was carved with delicate vines, geometric rosettes, and finished with smooth beeswax.

Abu Ahmad had an unyielding rule of life which he shared with his devoted wife: every day, he carved exactly two trays. In the evening, he took them to the bazaar and sold them for four silver dirhams.

Upon returning home, he meticulously divided the four dirhams into four equal portions: one dirham for their daily food of bread, oil, and lentils; one dirham for purchasing fresh timber for tomorrow’s work; one dirham for the rent of their modest cottage; and the fourth dirham was placed in a wooden box by the door to be distributed to the widows, orphans, and poor of the quarter before sunset.

One winter, a wealthy merchant offered Abu Ahmad ten times his usual wage if he would carve a hundred trays for an export caravan, working day and night.

Abu Ahmad smiled politely and declined the offer, saying: 'Brother, why should I burden my soul with haste and greed? Two trays a day provide our daily bread, sustain my craft, and allow us to feed the poor. If I hoard more, anxiety will steal my peace, and I shall have no time to reflect on the blessings of life.'

His wife supported his choice with all her heart. They lived in radiant peace, their cottage filled with the sweet fragrance of walnut wood and the smiles of grateful neighbors, proving that true wealth is not measured by the size of one’s storehouse, but by the balance and charity of one’s daily bread.
moral: Honest craftsmanship and systematic daily charity bring lasting contentment and heavenly blessings.
